doc.title: Sheila Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Middleburgh, New York, May 11, 2002

title: Hating to listen to her own recordings
summary: She rarely listens to her own records and recently revisited the Blue Note album.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Do you like to listen to your own recordings?

Hate it. Hate it. I hate it. I was sitting upstairs when this is how I don’t know my own — I only know it after I record it, go through the mixing, go through the listening to it back and then the final product I listen to it once or twice and then I never listen to it again unless it’s playing somewhere if I’m going to somebody’s house for a party or something and they have it on, I’ll say do you mind not playing that?

But just recently I did listen to Blue Note, the Blue Note recording. Because everybody was telling me, giving me really beautiful compliments on it, and I thought gee, what’s the big deal? I don’t — how come I don’t hear it? I don’t hear that. That doesn’t sound good to me. I mean I remember how I felt when I did it, but what happens is I start listening to it and I say, as most creative musicians, oh that could have gone here, and this could have gone there. You know I can’t just sit and enjoy it. Somebody else I can but we hear ourselves differently. But anyway I was upstairs while you all were getting ready to do this. And I heard this intro, and I thought oh my God that’s so beautiful. It was Kenny Barron. On “The Water is Wide.”
